h.strategy: Use retrieved findings to classify settings as strong, weak, neutral or harmful, and to identify which settings can disconnect other parts from the outcome. Propose hypotheses only of two kinds. Self-conditioning: the edit's effect depends on the value it replaces, being more negative when that value is strong and more positive when it is empty or harmful. Disconnection: when the edited part cannot influence the outcome, its effect shrinks toward zero, so the direction is lower if the edit usually helps and higher if it usually hurts. Directions refer to the signed effect. For each hypothesis, state the edit's usual sign and a one-sentence mechanism. Cover varied edit fields and values. The critic should replace any hypothesis with an uncertain usual sign, competing effects or reliance on partial redundancy.

hyps.why: With edge 0 none node 1 receives no input, so a conv on edge 2 is disconnected and its gain shrinks toward zero.
With edge 0 none edge 4 reads from a dead node 1 and cannot influence the output, so the conv gain vanishes.
Its source node 1 is dead when edge 0 is none, so the usual conv gain disappears.
A conv on the direct input-output edge gains most when it fills an empty slot rather than replacing another useful op.
Conv gain is largest when it replaces an empty edge rather than a skip or other conv.
Pool is a weak op, so replacing a strong conv_3x3 loses much more than replacing an empty or weak op.
Replacing none restores the whole feeder path into node 1, a far larger effect than skip swapping in for a real op.
Replacing a strong conv with a parameter-free skip costs accuracy, whereas skip over a weak or empty edge is neutral or positive.
Putting a conv on edge 0 over none activates node 1 and its downstream edges, so the gain exceeds conv_3x3 replacing another op.
A skip on edge 4 carries nothing from a dead node 1 when edge 0 is none, so its usual benefit is lost.
